blocks.heading: Preventing and resolving disputes
blocks.text: Clear communication, consultation, agreed responsibilities and fair procedures can help avoid unnecessary conflict. When relations break down, negotiation lets parties discuss differences and seek a mutually acceptable agreement. Collective bargaining is negotiation by unions and employers over pay and conditions; the syllabus glossary uses negotiation and collective bargaining as two names for the same process between management and workforce representatives. Arbitration involves an independent third party hearing both sides and giving a ruling. Begin by identifying the issue and parties, gathering relevant facts and using the agreed discussion arrangements. If direct agreement fails, an appropriate third-party route may help. Which method suits depends on the dispute.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Nela Foods’ management and worker representatives disagree over shift payments. They can share evidence and discuss proposals before considering an agreed independent ruling. Negotiation gives the parties a chance to reach their own settlement. Arbitration shifts the determination to a third party under the chosen arrangement, so it should not be described as merely another informal chat.

blocks.heading: Negotiation
blocks.text: Negotiation involves discussion and bargaining between parties seeking a mutually acceptable agreement. In the workplace, management and workforce representatives can clarify the issue, share information, exchange proposals and assess compromises. The parties themselves seek the settlement rather than asking an arbitrator to decide it. Clear authority to negotiate and reporting back to those represented matter.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Hila Foods’ management and staff representatives meet over shift arrangements. Sharing the staffing need and workers’ concerns can identify a workable rota. If they agree, record responsibilities and timing; a meeting without a settlement is not proof the conflict has ended.

blocks.heading: Collective bargaining
blocks.text: Collective bargaining is negotiations between one or more trade unions and one or more employers on pay and conditions of employment. It gives workers a representative collective voice rather than treating each employee as an isolated negotiator. Representatives should gather members’ priorities, discuss evidence with employers and communicate the outcome. Its scope can include a workplace or wider arrangements; do not assume every negotiation has identical participants.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: A union and employer discuss a proposed change in overtime payments. Because the union bargains collectively over employment conditions, this is collective bargaining. It remains negotiation, not an independent ruling.

blocks.heading: Arbitration
blocks.text: Arbitration means listening to both sides in an industrial dispute, trade union and management, and then giving a ruling of what the arbitrator thinks is fair to both sides. An independent third party considers evidence and determines an outcome under the chosen arrangement. This differs from direct negotiation where the parties seek their own agreement. Whether the ruling binds both sides depends on what they agreed beforehand.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: An employer and union cannot agree and accept an independent person to hear evidence and give a ruling. The third party’s determination identifies arbitration. Merely chairing a conversation without making a ruling would not be the same function.
